source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay (bioRxiv v4 PDF; Nat Neurosci 21:1609)
finding: The theory ranks every possible memory update (one Bellman backup) by its expected gain in future reward, called EVB. EVB is the product of gain and need. Backups run one at a time, best first.
numbers: Utility = gain x need. Computed separately for each backup (myopic). Zero gain or zero need gives zero utility.
quote: utility of a backup ... is the increase in reward at the target state multiplied by the expected number of times the target state will be visited
limits: Myopic: ignores that one backup can set up later backups. Normative, not a process model.
agent_relevance: Gives a direct rule to order stored subgoals: rank by (how much revisiting would change my plan) x (how likely I am to need that subgoal soon).

source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay (bioRxiv v4 PDF; Nat Neurosci 21:1609)
finding: Gain is the reward improvement from a policy change at the target state. It is zero if the update would not change the choice. Need is expected future occupancy of the state (discounted successor representation), so it favours the current state and states likely to come next.
numbers: Need = row of (I - T)^-1 for the current state (SR). Gain depends on how far the new value moves the best action; greedy agent: positive only if best action flips.
quote: a backup that has no effect on behavior has zero utility even if the target state is expected to be visited
limits: Gain needs the agent to know the policy effect before doing the backup; the authors call this unrealistic.
agent_relevance: Two separate scores to compute in code: policy-change value (gain) and expected re-use (need). A subgoal that would not change any decision should not be revisited.

source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay (bioRxiv v4 PDF; Nat Neurosci 21:1609)
finding: Simulation settings for the model, all fixed with no parameter fitting.
numbers: Gridworld, 4 moves. Softmax beta=5, discount gamma=0.9, learning rate alpha=1 (deterministic). 20 planning steps at the start and at the end of each episode. Minimum gain 1e-10 so all 20 steps are used. Reward noise SD 0.1. Transition model learning rate 0.9. 50 episodes per run. Dyna maze with obstacles, reward at (1,9); linear track as two 10-state segments.
limits: Model starts with a full transition model, so no exploration of memory contents is simulated. Only fixed deterministic tasks.
agent_relevance: Shows the policy needs only a small, fixed compute budget per pause (20 steps). A scaffold can set a similar fixed budget of revisits per pause.

source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay (bioRxiv v4 PDF; Nat Neurosci 21:1609)
finding: Learning is faster with prioritised replay than with no replay or random (original Dyna) replay, in both the open field and the linear track. A model-free agent still learns, only slower.
numbers: Fig 1d: steps-to-reward per episode over about 20 episodes (open field and track). No exact step counts in text.
limits: Curves only, no tabulated numbers in the text. Task is tiny.
agent_relevance: The efficiency gain over random revisit order is the core argument for ordering a subgoal library rather than sampling it uniformly.

source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay (bioRxiv v4 PDF; Nat Neurosci 21:1609)
finding: Direction of replay falls out of the two terms. After a surprise (prediction error) gain is largest behind the agent, so replay runs in reverse from the agent toward the start. Before a run need is largest ahead of the agent, so replay runs forward. Both are built by chaining backups, depth-first.
numbers: Significance by permutation test on runs of 5 or more backups. Linear track: forward events mostly before a run, reverse mostly after. Very few reverse before a run, very few forward after.
limits: Qualitative match to rodent data, no parameter fitting. Counts shown only as figures.
agent_relevance: Two modes for a thinking loop: after an unexpected result, walk backward through the steps that led there (credit assignment); before acting, walk forward through the likely path.

source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay (bioRxiv v4 PDF; Nat Neurosci 21:1609)
finding: Replay starts at or just behind the agent (initiation bias) and over-represents goal sites and the final turn toward the goal. The first 5 backups of forward events include future states and of reverse events include past states, above chance.
numbers: Model Fig 4a vs Davidson et al 2009 start distribution. Turning-point over-representation arises from the gain term near barriers.
limits: Fig 4 gives curves, no exact percentages in text. Forward-includes-future held even with randomised start locations (Fig S1).
agent_relevance: Start a revisit from the current state and bias toward decision points where a different choice would pay off.

source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay (bioRxiv v4 PDF; Nat Neurosci 21:1609)
finding: Offline replay (sleep, rest) is also predicted by the same rule. In a simulated T-maze with the agent absent, backups go mostly to the arm that was rewarded, as in the Olafsdottir et al 2015 preplay data.
numbers: Proportion of backups to cued arm much greater than uncued arm (Fig 4g,h). Need for the absent agent estimated as the stationary distribution of the transition model.
limits: Exact proportions not given in text. Single-reward T-maze.
agent_relevance: Idle time can be used to revisit the subgoals with highest expected value, not only the current one.

source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay (bioRxiv v4 PDF; Nat Neurosci 21:1609)
finding: Gain explains why reverse replay responds to reward change and forward replay does not. Learning that a good action is much worse has high gain; learning it is slightly worse (still best) has zero or negative gain. Simulated 4x and 0x reward tasks reproduce Ambrose et al 2016. Shock at the track end gives backup probability 1 at the shock zone after shock, versus negligible before.
numbers: Sim 4x reward: reverse events much larger for 4x than 1x, forward about equal. Sim 0x reward: reverse almost abolished, forward equal. Wu et al 2017 shock data compared.
limits: Zero-reward explanation also relies on the track structure (animal must reach the other end first, so propagating 0 has negative gain). Qualitative fit only.
agent_relevance: Do not revisit every bad outcome. Revisit only outcomes that would flip the choice. A bad result for an action that stays best anyway is low priority.

source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay (bioRxiv v4 PDF; Nat Neurosci 21:1609)
finding: Effect of experience: gain falls as prediction errors shrink, need rises as the route becomes predictable. So fewer events overall, but a given on-route state is more likely to be in an event.
numbers: Sim: significant events per trial fell from about 2 to about 0.8; forward from about 1.5 to 0.5; reverse from about 0.5 to 0.3. Compared with Cheng and Frank 2008 and O'Neill 2008 data.
limits: The literature is mixed on familiarity (increases and decreases both reported); model reconciles it qualitatively only.
agent_relevance: As a task is learned, revisit less often but more narrowly. Revisit rate should fall with prediction error.

source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay (bioRxiv v4 PDF; Nat Neurosci 21:1609)
finding: Compared with Prioritized Sweeping (large prediction error of either sign drives backups backward). The gain term predicts asymmetric effects of good and bad news, which PS cannot. The need term adds forward search and channels activity along used routes.
numbers: Argument rests on Ambrose 2016 asymmetry (Fig 5c-f).
limits: PS comparison is argued, not run as a head-to-head model fit.
agent_relevance: Plain error-size ranking (the default in AI replay) is a weaker rule than gain x need.

source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay (bioRxiv v4 PDF; Nat Neurosci 21:1609)
finding: Stated limits. Gain needs knowledge of the policy effect in advance. Tasks are stationary, deterministic and tiny. No uncertainty. Single scale of one-step backups. No mechanism for how the brain computes priority. Suggested approximation: myopic value of perfect information. Same priorities hold if replay updates a successor representation. Options would replay extended trajectories as units.
limits: Authors say the model does not give a process-level recipe.
agent_relevance: Cheap approximations to gain (does the update flip the best option?) will be needed. Subgoal options can be replayed as whole units.

source: Schaul, Quan, Antonoglou and Silver (2016) Prioritized Experience Replay (arXiv 1511.05952, ICLR 2016)
finding: Engineering version of prioritised access. Sample stored transitions by the size of their TD error, with stochastic sampling and importance-sampling correction. Greedy TD-error ordering over-fits to a few high-error items, is noise-sensitive, and starves items whose error was low on first visit.
numbers: Atari, 49 games: median human-normalised score DQN 48% -> 106% with rank-based PER; mean 122% -> 355%. Better than baseline on 41 of 49 games. Double DQN 57 games: median 111% -> 128%, mean 418% -> 551%. Learning about twice as fast. Chosen settings alpha=0.7 beta0=0.5 (rank), alpha=0.6 beta0=0.4 (proportional).
quote: replaying experience in the right order makes an enormous difference to the number of updates required
limits: Priority is error size only: no need term and no policy-change term. Mean score dominated by one game (Video Pinball).
agent_relevance: Order-of-revisit matters by orders of magnitude on sparse-reward problems; stochastic sampling avoids fixating on a few items. Error-size priority is the baseline gain x need should beat.

source: Moore and Atkeson (1993) Prioritized sweeping; Sutton (1991) Dyna (as described in Mattar and Daw 2018)
finding: Dyna learns from replayed or simulated experience between real steps. Prioritized sweeping orders those updates by prediction error, propagating surprise to predecessor states. Mattar and Daw treat both as special cases of their rule.
numbers: No numbers read from the original papers.
limits: Not opened in the original; second-hand from Mattar and Daw.
agent_relevance: Lineage for the Dyna-style offline loop; original papers still to open in a later pass.

source: Foster and Wilson (2006) Reverse replay of behavioural sequences in hippocampal place cells during the awake state (Nature)
finding: Rat hippocampus replays recent spatial runs in reversed order during awake pauses right after the run. The authors link it to evaluation of sequences in reinforcement learning models.
numbers: Abstract only.
quote: This replay is suggestive of a role in the evaluation of event sequences in the manner of reinforcement learning models.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC); no sample sizes read.
agent_relevance: Founding observation for: after a result, walk backward over the path.

source: Diba and Buzsaki (2007) Forward and reverse hippocampal place-cell sequences during ripples (Nat Neurosci)
finding: Place-cell sequences recur in reverse order at the end of a run and in forward order in anticipation of the run, both with sharp waves.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Abstract only; counts not read.
agent_relevance: Founding evidence for the forward-before, reverse-after split that gain and need explain.

source: Davidson, Kloosterman and Wilson (2009) Hippocampal replay of extended experience (Neuron)
finding: Rats on a 10.3 m linear track replay long runs. Replay can start remote from the rat and is compressed about 15-20 fold. Forward events outnumber reverse in this unpretrained, pausing set-up.
numbers: 4 rats, one session each. 263 significant events: 40% forward (106), 26% reverse (68), 33% mixed (89). Events over 250 ms: 48% forward (66/138), 25% reverse (34/138); forward more frequent p<0.005. 40% of trajectories start within 50 cm of the rat vs 17% chance. Median replay speed about 8.1 m/s.
limits: Four rats. p<0.01 threshold; at p<0.05, 29% of events qualify. Forward replay did not predict the actual next path (15 vs 12 cases) and reverse did not reliably match the path just taken (9 vs 7).
agent_relevance: Initiation bias source data. The finding that forward replay did not track the actual upcoming path is an early warning that replay content is not a direct plan.

source: Ambrose, Pfeiffer and Foster (2016) Reverse replay of hippocampal place cells is uniquely modulated by changing reward (Neuron)
finding: Only reverse replay changes its rate with reward size. Reverse replay rises when reward is raised and falls when removed; forward replay does not change reliably. This is the key asymmetry used to support gain.
numbers: 5 rats, CA1. Exp 1 (1x to 4x, 7 sessions): forward unchanged z=0.305 p=0.76; reverse between-end difference larger in unequal condition z=3.57 p=3.6e-4. Exp 2 (1x to 0x, 8 sessions): forward z=-1.83 p=0.068; reverse z=-2.05 p=0.041. 581/738 (79%) and 314/409 (77%) replays direction-classified.
quote: only reverse replays increased their rate at increased reward
limits: Very few replays at the zero-reward end; under stricter criteria no reverse replays there. Rats stayed longer at 4x (20.3 vs 8.1 s) and less at 0x (3.3 vs 8.5 s): dwell-time confound. Per-condition rates only in supplement. Forward replay peak before laps was not replicated. 5 rats.
agent_relevance: Backward revisit is tuned to reward news; forward revisit is not. Reward-change response is a signal for when to schedule backward credit assignment.

source: Karlsson and Frank (2009) Awake replay of remote experiences in the hippocampus (Nat Neurosci)
finding: Replay in awake rats is often of places they are not in, including a different, remote track. Replay of the novel track declines across the day.
numbers: 3 rats. Remote replay of E1 while in E2: 182/442 (41.2%), Z=12.67. Local replay 288/612 (47%). Awake rest-box replay 256/580 (44.1%); quiescent 373/1046 (35.7%), lower than awake Z=3.36 p<0.001. Final rest E1 replay 34.7% (51/147), decline p<0.04.
limits: 3 rats with different exposure histories. No EMG, so quiescent is not confirmed sleep. Correlation only. Depends on E1 being novel.
agent_relevance: Supports memory access to non-present items; offline revisits are normal. Replay frequency drifts down as an item becomes familiar, as gain predicts.

source: Pfeiffer and Foster (2013) Hippocampal place-cell sequences depict future paths to remembered goals (Nature)
finding: Before goal-directed movement in an open arena, hippocampal sequences run from the current location to the known goal and predict immediate behaviour, even for novel start-goal pairs.
numbers: Abstract only.
quote: these sequences predict immediate future behaviour, even in cases in which the specific combination of start and goal locations is novel
limits: Abstract only; Davidson 2009 and Gillespie 2021 report weaker prediction of upcoming choice.
agent_relevance: Main evidence for the need-driven forward mode: preview the path from here to the goal.

source: Gupta, van der Meer, Touretzky and Redish (2010) Hippocampal replay is not a simple function of experience (Neuron)
finding: Replay reflects all available paths, not recent or frequent ones. Replay of track B continued after more than 10 minutes of running A, B was replayed more when it was rare, and novel never-travelled paths were built.
numbers: Abstract only: B replayed after more than 10 min of A.
quote: replay of nonlocal sequence B occurred more often when B was infrequently experienced
limits: Abstract only. Rare-item replay is at odds with a pure need (frequency) account, closer to a coverage or gain account.
agent_relevance: A revisit schedule driven only by recent use will miss rarely used but valuable items.

source: Jadhav, Kemere, German and Frank (2012) Awake hippocampal sharp-wave ripples support spatial memory (Science)
finding: Causal test. Interrupting awake sharp-wave ripples impairs learning and performance on a spatial alternation task without disrupting place fields or post-experience reactivation.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Abstract only; effect sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Shows replay is causally useful for learning, so the ordering of what to replay is not just a side effect.

source: Widloski and Foster (2022) Flexible rerouting of hippocampal replay sequences around changing barriers (Neuron)
finding: When barriers and goals were moved, replays consistently depicted new goal-directed paths around the barriers and mostly avoided violating them. Place fields stayed stable; replay changed quickly.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Abstract only; counts not read.
agent_relevance: Evidence that revisits use the current model of constraints, not a stale cache.

source: Gillespie et al. (2021) Hippocampal replay reflects specific past experiences rather than a plan for subsequent choice (Neuron)
finding: Largest challenge to a pure planning reading. In an 8-arm win-stay/lose-switch task, replay content most reliably covered the previous goal, not the upcoming choice. Replay content did not track trial-by-trial behaviour.
numbers: 4 rats, 24-33 sessions each. Previous-goal replay about two-fold enriched; persisted for at least two subsequent blocks. Future-arm enrichment small, significant in 2/4 subjects (trial subsets) and 3/4 (GLM). Classifiers from replay counts predicting correct vs error trials at about 50% chance. Previous-goal replay vs later visits R2=0.008-0.023, p=0.49, 0.32, 0.18, 0.08.
quote: Replay content was decoupled from upcoming choice and reflected previously rewarded and non-recently visited locations
limits: 4 rats, dorsal CA1 only, correlational, weak trial-level effects (R2<0.03). Replay not split by direction. Authors cite Mattar and Daw only in Discussion; no formal gain or need test. They allow that routing to planning areas could still be selective.
agent_relevance: Failed or weak prediction for the forward-replay-is-a-plan reading. Treat gain x need as a design rule, not as proof the brain does exactly this. Replay of the previous goal fits a memory-storage role as well as value updating.

source: Momennejad, Otto, Daw and Norman (2018) Offline replay supports planning in human reinforcement learning (eLife)
finding: fMRI in humans. After a reward change, how strongly the old first-stage state is reinstated during rest predicts how well people re-plan. This is shown only where revaluation was needed.
numbers: 24 analysed. Two-stage task, revaluation vs control blocks. Replanning: revaluation t(23)=4.89 p<0.0001, control t(23)=-0.10. Rest reinstatement vs replanning: revaluation rho=0.54 p=0.0068; control rho=-0.13 p=0.55; difference p=0.023. Stage II replay not related (rho=0.2 p=0.17).
limits: Correlational. fMRI cannot see sub-second sequences. Noisy vs noiseless split underpowered (interaction p=0.34). Possible ceiling in noiseless blocks. Two-step tree only.
agent_relevance: Human evidence that offline revisit of the right state improves later choices after a change in value.

source: Momennejad et al. (2018) eLife - prediction-error tagging
finding: Unsigned prediction errors during learning predict which states are replayed later and replanned. Replay fades across rest periods as prediction errors shrink, in line with gain falling.
numbers: Conjunction of regions: ACC, mid-cingulate and precuneus, putamen. Revaluation replay fell from rest 1 to 3: t(23)=2.9 p=0.007. Rest 1 replay higher in revaluation than control t(23)=2.17 p=0.039. Learning rate 0.7 (pilot) and 0.78 (fMRI sample), gamma=1.
limits: Signed and unsigned prediction errors highly correlated, cannot be separated. Conjunction significant only in pooled blocks. Cannot tell tagging at encoding from later search.
agent_relevance: Prediction error is a real part of the priority signal in people; log surprise per stored item.

source: Eldar, Lievre, Dayan and Dolan (2020) The roles of online and offline replay in planning (eLife)
finding: MEG, 40 people, 8-state task. Replay appeared right after surprising outcomes (online) and during rest (offline). Online replay followed policy-relevant news and preceded policy change. No formal gain or need test, but the authors call the data broadly consistent with Mattar and Daw.
numbers: N=40. Online: forward sequenceness lag 130 ms; predicted by flexibility index beta=0.17, surprise beta=0.06, interaction beta=0.19. Moves with high forward sequenceness less likely re-chosen (rho=-0.04 p=0.04, n=25); re-evaluation raised reward by 11.1% (p=0.001). Offline (frequent transitions) sequenceness 0.002 p=0.01, lag 180 ms, forward; infrequent transitions 0.000 p=0.47. Hybrid MF-MB model best BIC 39908.
limits: No gain/need test run. Preplay at choice not detected. Correlational. Offline sequenceness correlated negatively with flexibility. N=40.
agent_relevance: Suggests both surprise-triggered and idle-time revisits, and that they relate to policy change.

source: Liu, Mattar, Behrens, Daw and Dolan (2021) Experience replay is associated with efficient nonlocal learning (Science)
finding: First direct human test of the gain x need prediction. MEG during a path-learning task: backward replay at reward (160 ms lag) of non-local paths was stronger for high-utility paths and linked to faster non-local learning.
numbers: N=29 (power for d=0.5). Need set by arm frequency 17/33/50%; gain from model, drifting end-state reward 25-75%. Need and gain uncorrelated r=-0.004. 160 ms backward replay: non-local content t(28)=2.92 p=0.007; high vs low utility t(28)=3.30 p=0.003. Need-only or gain-only comparisons did not show it. 30 ms forward replay: no non-local content, no utility effect (p=0.74). Learning rate 0.70 with 160 ms replay vs 0.61 without (p=0.023). Across subjects replay vs reward per trial r=0.41 p=0.03.
limits: Correlational. Gain estimated from a model and partly depends on participants' own choices. Only the product was prioritised, neither term alone. p values near threshold. Decoding peak 47% (chance 6%). Forward replay at choice showed no credit-assignment role here.
agent_relevance: Best direct support that the product (not either term alone) predicts what is replayed. It also gives forward replay no role in this task.

source: Liu et al. (2021) Science - gain and need split
finding: Learning from the non-local path depended on gain more than need.
numbers: High-gain non-local paths learned faster: alpha 0.79 vs 0.37, p=0.020. High-need: 0.61 vs 0.54, p=0.16. Local vs non-local learning rates similar: 0.64 vs 0.60, p=0.61. Replay strength not explained by encounter frequency p=0.59/0.54.
limits: Gain from fitted model; N=29; need effect not significant.
agent_relevance: Weight the gain term heavily; need alone was not a reliable driver here.

source: Annual Review of Neuroscience (2026) Planning in the Brain: It's Not What You Think It Is
finding: Review frames replay as selectively prioritised by expected learning benefit (metacontrol), citing Mattar and Daw 2018 as the key model. Also lists doubts: replay timing and content are not reliably tied to later choices, can lag learning, and cached results can go stale.
numbers: No effect sizes. Cites Carey 2019, Gillespie 2021 (weak choice link), Gupta 2010 (novel paths), Momennejad 2018, Kurth-Nelson 2015, Liu 2021. Cites Jensen et al 2024: metalearned policy for when to start rollouts resembles replay.
limits: Review says evidence was combined somewhat breezily and mechanisms may not be unitary. Does not state the gain x need formula itself.
agent_relevance: Current field view: prioritisation is plausible but not settled; stale cache is a named risk, which maps to our staleness guardrail.

source: Ma et al. (2026) Freshness-Aware Prioritized Experience Replay for LLM/VLM RL (FreshPER, arXiv 2604.16918)
finding: Plain prioritised replay fails when applied to LLM reinforcement learning because stored priorities go stale as the policy changes. Multiplying priority by an exponential age decay fixes this. This is a need-like term (is it still relevant now).
numbers: Qwen2.5 0.5B, 3B-VL, 7B; eight tasks. Peak gains over on-policy: NQ Search +46%, Sokoban Simple +367%, VLM FrozenLake +133%, AIME +18%. Standard PER (priority = |reward|) underperformed on-policy on most tasks, catastrophically on Sokoban Simple and NQ Search. Defaults: buffer 50K trajectories, alpha=0.6, beta=0.4, decay constant 500 (1000 for AIME).
quote: Standard PER without age decay consistently degrades performance
limits: Training-time replay on model weights, not a scaffold at inference. Reward-magnitude priority only; no policy-change gain term. Percent gains on small baselines (Sokoban). Preprint.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as the brain model: pure error-size priority picks stale items. Age or relevance weighting must multiply the priority.

source: Yoo et al. (2026) Rollout-Level Advantage-Prioritized Experience Replay for GRPO (arXiv 2606.04560)
finding: Replaying individual rollouts ranked by absolute advantage, with an age cap and fresh on-policy data kept in each batch, beats GRPO at three scales. Mixing stale and fresh rollouts without anchoring falls below GRPO at 4B.
numbers: Qwen3-Base 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B; five math benchmarks. Average gains +0.61, +0.60 and +1.66 points. Best age cap 10 training steps; replay ratio 0.5.
limits: Small gains in points. Training-time method. Priority is advantage magnitude, which is gain-like (how much signal), with an age cap that is need-like.
agent_relevance: Gain-like priority plus a hard staleness cap is the working pattern in LLM RL.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Enhancing LLM Agents for Code Generation with Possibility and Pass-rate Prioritized Experience Replay (arXiv 2410.12236)
finding: Failed programs from beam-search sampling are stored and replayed in fine-tuning, ranked by P2Value (model probability times test pass rate). Reported to improve several code LLMs on APPS, CodeContests and HumanEval.
numbers: Value combines token possibility and pass rate; sampled with probabilities from P2Value. Benchmarks: APPS, CodeContests, HumanEval (164 problems). Clean headline numbers not extracted from the PDF text.
limits: Training-time. Gain numbers not reliably read in this pass. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Near-miss attempts (high partial pass rate) are worth revisiting; a priority from partial test results is cheap to compute.
